passages.text: And thereat they parted for that time, and all men went back to their booths.

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text: But on the second day after this it was made law in the law-court that, henceforth, all holmgangs should be forbidden; and this was done by the counsel of all the wisest men that were at the Thing; and there, indeed, were all the men of most counsel in the land. And this was the last holmgang fought in Iceland, this, wherein Gunnlaug and Raven fought.

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text: But this Thing was the third most thronged Thing that has been held in Iceland; the first was after Njal's burning, the second after the Heath-slaughters.

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text: Now, one morning, as the brothers Hermund and Gunnlaug went to Axe-water to wash, on the other side went many women towards the river, and in that company was Helga the Fair. Then said Hermund:

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text: Dost thou see thy friend Helga there on the other side of the river?

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text: Surely, I see her, says Gunnlaug, and withal he sang:

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text:
Born was she for men's bickering:
Sore bale hath wrought the war-stem,
And I yearned every madly
To hold that oak-tree golden.
To me then, me destroyer
Of swan-mead's flame, uneedful
This looking on the dark-eyed,
This golden land's beholding.
lines: Born was she for men's bickering:
Sore bale hath wrought the war-stem,

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text: Therewith the crossed the river, and Helga and Gunnlaug spake awhile together, and as the brothers crossed the river eastward back again, Helga stood and gazed long after Gunnlaug.

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text: Then Gunnlaug looked back and sang:

passages.chapter_title: Of the holmgang at the Althing
passages.text:
Moon of linen-lapped one,
Leek-sea-bearing goddess,
Hawk-keen out of heaven
Shone all bright upon me;
But that eyelid's moonbeam
Of gold-necklaced goddess
Her hath all undoing
Wrought, and me made nought of.
lines: Wrought, and me made nought of.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: Now after these things were gone by men rode home from the Thing, and Gunnlaug dwelt at home at Gilsbank.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: On a morning when he awoke all men had risen up, but he alone still lay abed; he lay in a shut-bed behind the seats. Now into the hall came twelve men, all full armed, and who should be there but Raven, Onund's son; Gunnlaug sprang up forthwith, and got to his weapons.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: But Raven spake, Thou art in risk of no hurt this time, quoth he, but my errand hither is what thou shalt now hear: Thou didst call me to a holmgang last summer at the Althing, and thou didst not deem matters to be fairly tried therein; now I will offer thee this, that we both fare away from Iceland, and go abroad next summer, and go on holm in Norway, for there our kinsmen are not like to stand in our way.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: Gunnlaug answered, Hail to thy words, stoutest of men! this thine offer I take gladly; and here, Raven, mayest thou have cheer as good as thou mayest desire.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: It is well offered, said Raven, but this time we shall first have to ride away. Thereon they parted.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: Now the kinsmen of both sore misliked them of this, but could in no wise undo it, because of the wrath of Gunnlaug and Raven; and, after all, that must betide that drew towards.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: Now it is to be said of Raven that he fitted out his ship in Leiruvag; two men are named that went with him, sisters' sons of his father Onund, one hight Grim, the other Olaf, doughty men both. All the kinsmen of Raven thought it great scathe when he went away, but he said he had challenged Gunnlaug to the holmgang because he could have no joy soever of Helga; and he said, withal, that one must fall before the other.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: So Raven put to sea, when he had wind at will, and brought his ship to Thrandheim, and was there that winter and heard nought of Gunnlaug that winter through; there he abode him the summer following: and still another winter was he in Thrandheim, at a place called Lifangr.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: Gunnlaug Worm-tongue took ship with Hallfred Troublous-Skald, in the north at The Plain; they were very late ready for sea.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: They sailed into the main when they had a fair wind, and made Orkney a little before the winter. Earl Sigurd Lodverson was still lord over the isles, and Gunnlaug went to him and abode there that winter, and the earl held him of much account.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: In the spring the earl would go on warfare, and Gunnlaug made ready to go with him; and that summer they harried wide about the South-isles and Scotland's firths, and had many fights, and Gunnlaug always showed himself the bravest and doughtiest of fellows, and the hardiest of men wherever they came.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: Earl Sigurd went back home early in the summer, but Gunnlaug took ship with chapmen, sailing for Norway, and he and Earl Sigurd parted in great friendship.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: Gunnlaug fared north to Thrandheim, to Hladir, to see Earl Eric, and dwelt there through the early winter; the earl welcomed him gladly, and made offer to Gunnlaug to stay with him, and Gunnlaug agreed thereto.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: The earl had heard already how all had befallen between Gunnlaug and Raven, and he told Gunnlaug that he laid ban on their fighting within his realm; Gunnlaug said the earl should be free to have his will herein.

passages.chapter_title: How Gunnlaug and Raven agreed to go East To Norway, to try the matter again
passages.text: So Gunnlaug abode there the winter through, ever heavy of mood.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: But on a day in spring Gunnlaug was walking abroad, and his kinsman Thorkel with him; they walked away from the town, till on the meads before them they saw a ring of men, and in that ring were two men with weapons fencing; but one was named Raven, the other Gunnlaug, while they who stood by said that Icelanders smote light, and were slow to remember their words.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Gunnlaug saw the great mocking hereunder, and much jeering was brought into the play; and withal he went away silent.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: So a little while after he said to the earl that he had no mind to bear any longer the jeers and mocks of his courtiers about his dealings with Raven, and therewith he prayed the earl to give him a guide to Lifangr: now before this the earl had been told that Raven had left Lifangr and gone east to Sweden; therefore, he granted Gunnlaug leave to go, and gave him two guides for the journey.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Now Gunnlaug went from Hladir with six men to Lifangr; and, on the morning of the very day whereas Gunnlaug came in in the evening, Raven had left Lifangr with four men. Thence Gunnlaug went to Vera-dale, and came always in the evening to where Raven had been the night before.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: So Gunnlaug went on till he came to the uppermost farm in the valley, called Sula, wherefrom had Raven fared in the morning; there he stayed not his journey, but kept on his way through the night.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Then in the morning at sunrise they saw one another. Raven had got to a place where were two waters, and between them flat meads, and they are called Gleipni's meads: but into one water stretched a little ness called Dingness. There on the ness Raven and his fellows, five together, took their stand. With Raven were his kinsmen, Grim and Olaf.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Now when they met, Gunnlaug said, It is well that we have found one another.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Raven said that he had nought to quarrel with therein; But now, says he, thou mayest choose as thou wilt, either that we fight alone together, or that we fight all of us man to man.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Gunnlaug said that either way seemed good to him.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Then spake Raven's kinsmen, Grim and Olaf, and said that they would little like to stand by and look on the fight, and in like wise spake Thorkel the Black, the kinsman of Gunnlaug.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Then said Gunnlaug to the earl's guides, Ye shall sit by and aid neither side, and be here to tell of our meeting; and so they did.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: So they set on, and fought dauntlessly, all of them. Grim and Olaf went both against Gunnlaug alone, and so closed their dealings with him that Gunnlaug slew them both and got no wound. This proves Thord Kolbeinson in a song that he made on Gunnlaug the Worm-tongue: ----

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text:
Grim and Olaf, great-hearts
In Gondul's din, with thin sword
First did Gunnlaug fell there
Ere at Raven fared he;
Bold, with blood be-drifted
Bane of three the thane was;
War-lord of the wave-horse
Wrought for men folks' slaughter.
lines: In Gondul's din, with thin sword
Bane of three the thane was;

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Meanwhile Raven and Thorkel the Black, Gunnlaug's kinsman, fought until Thorkel fell before Raven and lost his life; and so at last all their fellowship fell. Then they two alone fought together with fierce onsets and mighty strokes, which they dealt each the other, falling on furiously without stop or delay.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Gunnlaug had the sword Ethelred's-gift, and that was the best of weapons. At last Gunnlaug dealt a mighty blow at Raven, and cut his leg from under him; but none the more did Raven fall, but swung round up to a tree-stem, whereat he steadied the stump.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Then said Gunnlaug, Now thou art no more meet for battle, nor will I fight thee any longer, a maimed man.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Raven answered: So it is, said he, that my lot is now all the worser lot, but it were well with me yet, might I but drink somewhat.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Gunnlaug said, Betray me not if I bring thee water in my helm.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: I will not betray thee, said Raven.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Then went Gunnlaug to a brook and fetched water in his helm, and brought it to Raven; but Raven stretched forth his left hand to take it, but with his right hand drave his sword into Gunnlaug's head, and that was a mighty great wound.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Then Gunnlaug said, Evilly hast thou beguiled me, and done traitorously wherein I trusted thee.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Raven answers, Thou sayest sooth, but this brought me to it, that I begrudged thee to lie in the bosom of Helga the Fair.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Thereat they fought on, recking of nought; but the end of it was that Gunnlaug overcame Raven, and there Raven lost his life.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: Then the earl's guides came forward and bound the head-wound of Gunnlaug, and in meanwhile he sat and sang:

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text:
O thou sword-storm stirrer,
Raven, stem of battle
Famous, fared against me
Fiercely in the spear din.
Many a flight of metal
Was borne on me this morning,
By the spear-walls' builder,
Ring-bearer, on hard Dingness.
lines: Was borne on me this morning,

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: After that they buried the dead, and got Gunnlaug on to his horse thereafter, and brought him right down to Lifangr. There he lay three nights, and got all his rights of a priest , and died thereafter, and was buried at the church there.

passages.chapter_title: How the two foes met and fought at Dingness
passages.text: All men thought it great scathe of both of these men, Gunnlaug and Raven, amid such deeds as they died.

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: Now this summer, before these tidings were brought out hither to Iceland, Illugi the Black, being at home at Gilsbank, dreamed a dream: he thought that Gunnlaug came to him in his sleep, all bloody, and he sang in the dream this stave before him; and Illugi remembered the song when he woke, and sang it before others:

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text:
Knew I of the hewing
Of Raven's hilt-finned steel-fish
Byrny-shearing----sword-edge
Sharp clave leg of Raven. ----
Of warm wounds drank the eagle,
When the war-rod slender,
Cleaver of the corpses,
Clave the head of Gunnlaug.
lines: Of warm wounds drank the eagle,

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: This portent befel south at Mossfell, the selfsame night, that Onund dreamed how Raven came to him, covered all over with blood, and sang:

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text:
Red is the sword, but I now
Am undone by Sword-Odin.
'Gainst shields beyond the sea-flood
The ruin of shields was wielded.
Methinks the blood-fowl blood-stained
In blood o'er men's heads stood there,
The wound-erne yet wound-eager
Trod over wounded bodies.
lines: Red is the sword, but I now
The ruin of shields was wielded.
In blood o'er men's heads stood there,

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: Now the second summer after this, Illugi the Black spoke at the Althing from the Hill of Laws, and said:

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: Wherewith wilt thou make atonement to me for my son, whom Raven, thy son, beguiled in his troth?

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: Onund answers, Be it far from me to atone for him, so sorely as their meeting hath wounded me. Yet will I not ask atonement of thee for my son.

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: Then shall my wrath come home to some of thy kin, says Illugi. And withal after the Thing was Illugi at most times very sad.

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: Tells the tale how this autumn Illugi rode from Gilsbank with thirty men, and came to Mossfell early in the morning. Then Onund got into the church with his sons, and took sanctuary; but Illugi caught two of his kin, one called Biorn and the other Thorgrim, and had Biorn slain, but the feet smitten from Thorgrim. And thereafter Illugi rode home, and there was no righting of this for Onund.

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: Hermund, Illugi's son, had little joy after the death of Gunnlaug his brother, and deemed he was none the more avenged even though this had been wrought.

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: Now there was a man called Raven, brother's son to Onund of Mossfell; he was a great seafarer, and had a ship that lay up in Ramfirth: and in the spring Hermund Illugison rode from home alone north over Holt-beacon Heath, even to Ramfirth, and out as far as Board-ere to the ship of the chapmen. The chapmen were then nearly ready for sea; Raven, the ship-master, was on shore, and many men with him; Hermund rode up to him, and thrust him through with his spear, and rode away forthwith: but all Raven's men were bewildered at seeing Hermund.

passages.chapter_title: The news of the fight brought to Iceland
passages.text: No atonement came for this slaying, and there with ended the dealings of Illugi the Black and Onund of Mossfell.

passages.chapter_title: The death of Helga the Fair
passages.text: As time went on, Thorstein Egilson married his daughter Helga to a man called Thorkel, son of Hallkel, who lived west in Hraundale. Helga went to his house with him, but loved him little, for she cannot cease to think of Gunnlaug, though he be dead. Yet was Thorkel a doughty man, and wealthy of goods, and a good skald.

passages.chapter_title: The death of Helga the Fair
passages.text: They had children together not a few, one of them was called Thorarin, another Thorstein, and yet more they had.

passages.chapter_title: The death of Helga the Fair
passages.text: But Helga's chief joy was to pluck at the threads of that cloak, Gunnlaug's-gift, and she would be ever gazing at it.

passages.chapter_title: The death of Helga the Fair
passages.text: But on a time there came a great sickness to the house of Thorkel and Helga, and many were bed-ridden for a long time. Helga also fell sick, and yet she could not keep abed.

passages.chapter_title: The death of Helga the Fair
passages.text: So one Saturday evening Helga sat in the firehall, and leaned her head upon her husband's knees, and had the cloak Gunnlaug's-gift sent for; and when the cloak came to her she sat up and plucked at it, and gazed thereon awhile, and then sank back upon her husband's bosom, and was dead. Then Thorkel sang this:

passages.chapter_title: The death of Helga the Fair
passages.text:
Dead in mine arms she droopeth,
My dear one, gold-rings bearer,
For God hath changed the life-days
Of this Lady of the linen.
Weary pain hath pined her,
But unto me, the seeker
Of hoard of fishes highway,
Abiding here is wearier.
lines: Dead in mine arms she droopeth,
For God hath changed the life-days
Of this Lady of the linen.

passages.chapter_title: The death of Helga the Fair
passages.text: Helga was buried in the church there, but Thorkel dwelt yet at Hraundale: but a great matter seemed the death of Helga to all, as was to be looked for.

passages.chapter_title: The death of Helga the Fair
passages.text: And here endeth the story.
